932.title: Mirabai's songs
932.hook: a woman who left a palace counts her treasure
932.howItsDone: Payoji maine Ram ratan dhan payo is sung as a bhajan at home gatherings, in temples and on concert stages, and in school and community prayer meetings in India.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mirabai's songs: mine is Giridhar Gopal, and no one else. Whose did you walk in as? Day nine hundred thirty-two.

A strange inventory for a princess. Mira grew up, the stories say, among jewels and silks, in a house with a treasury. She walked away from all of it. And one of the songs sung in her voice is about getting rich. Payoji maine Ram ratan dhan payo. I've found it, I've found the treasure, the jewel of Ram's name. A woman who left a royal house describes what she has now in the language of money. Today, our last day with Mira: her accounts.
screen: `JEWELS, SILKS, A TREASURY.` → `SHE WALKS AWAY.` → `I'VE FOUND THE TREASURE.`

segments.voice: Listen to it like a statement from the bank. Credit: a priceless thing, given to me by my true guru, out of kindness. Balance: the savings of lifetime after lifetime, found at last. Debit: everything else the world offered, gone. Then come the terms of the account, terms no bank has ever offered. Spend it, and it doesn't run down. Thieves can't touch it. Day by day it grows. And then the song leaves the bank for a river. The boat is truth, the boatman is the true guru, and I have crossed the ocean of becoming. The last line: Mira's lord is Giridhar, and she sings his praise with joy upon joy. Two things are worth noticing. First, the names. Mira's beloved is Krishna, the mountain-lifter. Here she sings of the jewel of Ram's name. Some readers hear Ram's name here as the name of God itself, and the very last line still calls her lord Giridhar. The song holds both names without strain. Second, the treasure is given, not earned. A guru hands it over in kindness. All her own effort in the song is the receiving and the singing. Look at Mira's three days together. A cup of poison she drank laughing. A husband she chose against the world's shame. And now the ledger of a woman who lost a palace and counts herself rich, because she owns the one thing that grows when it's spent.
screen: `READ IT LIKE A BANK STATEMENT.` · `SPENT, IT DOESN'T RUN DOWN.` · `THE BOAT IS TRUTH.` · then, large: `THE ONE THING THAT GROWS WHEN SPENT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe, and make a quiet ledger. On one side, something you've lost or let go of: a plan, a place, an earlier version of yourself. Don't hurry past it. On the other side, ask: is there something I have that spending doesn't use up? A love, a kindness someone once gave you, a practice, a faith, a name you say. Hold that one. Notice that sitting with it doesn't make it any smaller. If you pray, you can thank the one who gave it to you. The bell holds the time.
Mirabai's songs. In this one, the jewel of the name: a treasure no thief can steal, which grows each day it's spent.
Your line: Mirabai's songs. Today, spend something that grows when it's spent, like attention, patience or a kind word, and see whether you run out. Day nine hundred thirty-two.

933.title: Chaitanya and the Bengal kirtan
933.hook: a grammar teacher whose every lesson turns into Krishna
933.howItsDone: In Gaudiya Vaishnava temples and homes, kirtan is sung with drums and hand cymbals, one voice leading and the group answering, and street processions of chanting, called nagar kirtan, still pass through towns and cities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mirabai's songs counted a treasure that grows when it's spent. What did you spend? Day nine hundred thirty-three.

A grammar teacher in Bengal has a problem. His students come to learn Sanskrit grammar, and every rule he explains turns into Krishna. A verb ending? Krishna. A noun? One of Krishna's names. Tradition says this young teacher, called Nimai, was known in his town of Navadvipa as a brilliant scholar and a fierce debater. Then he went on pilgrimage to Gaya, and came home unable to talk about anything else. His students, the story goes, finally closed their books and left. He let them go. He had found something louder than grammar.
screen: `A GRAMMAR TEACHER IN BENGAL.` → `EVERY RULE TURNS INTO KRISHNA.` → `THE STUDENTS CLOSE THEIR BOOKS.`

segments.voice: Nimai is the man remembered as Chaitanya. Back home, he and his friends began to gather at night in the courtyard of a devotee named Shrivasa, doors shut, singing God's names together. Drums, hand cymbals, one voice leading and everyone answering. That's kirtan: praise sung out loud, together, the names repeated again and again. Then the doors opened. Chaitanya's companions took the singing into the lanes of Navadvipa, a procession of drums and cymbals moving from house to house, and whoever heard it could fall in behind. At the center of it, his tradition places one chant: Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare. Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare. Nothing but names, calling and calling. What's radical is how little it asks. No Sanskrit grammar. No years of study. No temple door to get through. You need a voice, or even just ears and the willingness to answer the line that's sung to you. A scholar who could out-argue his town set down the argument and picked up the drum. His followers in Bengal, the Gaudiya Vaishnavas, remember him dancing as he sang, weeping, falling to the ground, his whole body caught up in the names. They also hold that he was more than a saint: Krishna himself, joined with Radha, come to taste his own love from the inside. Others honor him as a great teacher of devotion. Either way, what he gave the street was the same: a song anyone could join on the first try.
screen: `NIGHTS IN SHRIVASA'S COURTYARD.` · `THE DOORS OPEN TO THE LANES.` · `NOTHING BUT NAMES.` · then, large: `A SONG ANYONE CAN JOIN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath find its rhythm. Kirtan is a call and an answer, so let your breath do both. The out-breath is the leader's line. The in-breath is the crowd, answering. If you'd like, hum softly on the out-breath, or whisper a name that matters to you, and let the in-breath be the pause where the answer comes back. If you pray, you can use a name of God you already know. If not, a single soft sound is enough. Keep the call and answer going, gently. The bell holds the time.
Chaitanya and the Bengal kirtan. A scholar who set down his arguments and took the singing of God's names out of a closed courtyard and into the street.
screen: `CHAITANYA AND THE BENGAL KIRTAN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Chaitanya and the Bengal kirtan. Today, join something you'd usually only watch: a song, a chorus, a cheer, even one line of it. Day nine hundred thirty-three.

934.title: Chaitanya and the Bengal kirtan
934.hook: humbler than a blade of grass, more patient than a tree
934.howItsDone: Gaudiya Vaishnavas recite the Shikshashtakam, and the grass-and-tree verse is often sung or quoted before kirtan; at Puri's Ratha Yatra, kirtan groups sing and dance before Jagannath's chariot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chaitanya and the Bengal kirtan: a scholar set down his arguments and took God's names into the street. What did you join? Day nine hundred thirty-four.
screen: `CHAITANYA AND THE BENGAL KIRTAN.` · `A SONG ANYONE CAN JOIN.`

segments.voice: Step on a blade of grass and it bends flat. Lift your foot and, after a moment, it stands back up. No complaint, no grudge. A tree does something similar in the heat: it stands in the sun all day and gives its shade to whoever sits down, including the one with the axe. Those two humble things, grass and a tree, open a short verse that Chaitanya's tradition treasures. Today, on the last day of the saints of bhakti, it answers a practical question: how do you keep singing?
screen: `GRASS BENDS, THEN STANDS.` → `A TREE GIVES ITS SHADE.` → `HOW DO YOU KEEP SINGING?`

segments.voice: Chaitanya's followers keep a short set of verses under his name, called the Shikshashtakam, his teaching. One of them goes, in plain English: be humbler than a blade of grass, more patient than a tree. Give honor to others, and ask none for yourself. Then you can sing the name of Hari always. Read it as the fine print under yesterday's kirtan. Anyone can join the song on the first try. Staying in it is harder. Pride wants the lead line. Impatience wants the song to end. Wanting respect turns a chorus into a competition. The verse clears all three away, and what's left can keep singing. His tradition remembers him living it out in Puri, on the coast, where he spent his later years near the temple of Jagannath. At the great chariot festival, the Ratha Yatra, he is remembered dancing in front of the rolling chariot with groups of kirtan singers, lost in the names, the whole crowd caught up with him. Now look back at the road we've walked these four weeks. Andal and Nammalvar, singing to Vishnu in Tamil. The Nayanars, singing to Shiva. Jnaneshwar, Namdev and Tukaram, walking and singing in Maharashtra. Kabir and his sharp couplets. Tulsidas and Hanuman's song. Surdas in Yashoda's yard. Mira, laughing over the cup. And Chaitanya in the street with a drum. Different languages, different names for God. One habit: they sang to God as if God were near. Next, the modern teachers, beginning with a temple priest near Calcutta and a schoolteacher with a notebook.
screen: `HUMBLER THAN GRASS.` · `MORE PATIENT THAN A TREE.` · `DANCING BEFORE THE CHARIOT.` · then, large: `THEY SANG AS IF GOD WERE NEAR.`

segments.voice: Sit, and feel where your body meets the floor or the chair. For a minute, be like grass: low, rooted, flexible. Breathe in, and as you breathe out, let go of one small need to be right, or to be noticed, today. Breathe in again. Now be like the tree, standing in the sun so others can rest in your shade. Bring to mind one person you could honor today without needing anything back. Hold them in your attention. If you pray, you can let a name of God ride gently on the breath. The bell holds the time.
Chaitanya and the Bengal kirtan. The song in the street, and the fine print that keeps it going: humbler than grass, more patient than a tree.

935.title: Ramakrishna (the Gospel, selections)
935.hook: a schoolteacher with a notebook, and a priest who asks who weeps for God
935.carry: I'd die for one breath of air
935.howItsDone: The Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna is read aloud in study circles and at Ramakrishna centers, and devotees visit the temple garden at Dakshineswar, where his room is kept.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chaitanya and the Bengal kirtan: humbler than grass, more patient than a tree. Whom did you honor without asking anything back? Day nine hundred thirty-five.
screen: `CHAITANYA AND THE BENGAL KIRTAN.` · `HUMBLER THAN GRASS.`

segments.voice: A schoolteacher keeps a diary. That sounds like nothing. But this one comes home from visits to a temple garden north of Calcutta and writes down, as exactly as he can, what a priest there said that day: the jokes, the songs, the questions, who was sitting in the room. He signs his work with a single letter: M. Those pages became a book in Bengali, the Kathamrita, and in English, the Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna. Today a new stretch begins, the modern teachers, and it begins with the man in that room.
screen: `A SCHOOLTEACHER KEEPS A DIARY.` → `HE SIGNS IT: M.` → `THE MAN IN THAT ROOM.`

segments.voice: Ramakrishna served as a priest at the Kali temple at Dakshineswar, on the bank of the Ganges. The stories about him keep returning to one thing: he longed for God, for the Divine Mother, with an intensity that alarmed the people around him. Tradition says that as a young priest he would weep at the end of a day: another day gone, Mother, and still you haven't shown yourself. Years later, when visitors came to his room, some of them educated men from the city, he kept coming back to that longing. In the Gospel he says, in effect: people shed jugs of tears over their wives and children, over money and property. Who weeps for God? And he tells a story. A disciple asked his teacher how to see God. Come with me, the teacher said, and walked him to a pond, and pushed his head under the water. Held it there. Then let him up, gasping. What did you feel? I felt I'd die for one breath of air. When you long for God like that, the teacher said, you will see God. It's an alarming story, and it's meant to be. It isn't a method; nobody is being told to hold anyone's head under water. It's a measurement. How much do you want this? In these sayings, Ramakrishna's answer comes back to longing. Not cleverness first, not learning first. Wanting God the way lungs want air. And M. himself? He signs as a single letter, a quiet man with a notebook, so the voice that fills the room is the priest's.
screen: `A PRIEST AT DAKSHINESWAR.` · `WHO WEEPS FOR GOD?` · `A HEAD HELD UNDER WATER.` · then, large: `WANT GOD THE WAY LUNGS WANT AIR.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe slowly, and notice the next breath arriving. Don't hold it. Just notice how completely the body wants air, without ever being taught. Then ask: what do I want, underneath everything, the way my lungs want this breath? If you pray, it may be God. It may be peace, or someone's healing, or a life that means something. Name it plainly to yourself. Let the wanting be honest, not polite. Then rest with it, breath after breath. The bell holds the time.
Ramakrishna. The priest of the Kali temple at Dakshineswar, whose conversations M. wrote down, and who asked: who weeps for God?
Your line: I'd die for one breath of air. Today, notice one thing you want the way lungs want air, and give it five honest minutes. Day nine hundred thirty-five.

936.title: Ramakrishna (the Gospel, selections)
936.hook: a snake promises not to bite, and the village boys find out
936.carry: I never told you not to hiss
936.howItsDone: Ramakrishna's parables, like the snake that was told not to bite, are retold in talks and study circles at Ramakrishna Math and Mission centers, often as practical guidance for people living family lives.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramakrishna asked who weeps for God, and told of a head held under water, and your line, I'd die for one breath of air. What did you want the way lungs want air? Day nine hundred thirty-six.

A village path has a problem: a snake lives beside it, and it bites. People take the long way around. Then a holy man comes walking down that path, unafraid, and the snake rises to strike. He calms it with a few words and gives it a teaching. Ramakrishna told this story in his room at Dakshineswar to visitors who lived ordinary lives, with jobs, families and difficult neighbors. It's a funny story, and it's about a problem gentle people can run into.
screen: `A SNAKE BY THE VILLAGE PATH.` → `A HOLY MAN, UNAFRAID.` → `A TEACHING FOR A SNAKE.`

segments.voice: The holy man gives the snake a sacred name to repeat and tells it: stop biting. Harm no one. The snake takes it to heart, and stops. Soon the village boys notice that the dangerous snake is harmless now. They throw stones at it. They grab it by the tail, whirl it around and dash it on the ground. The snake drags itself, half dead, into its hole, and lives on scraps. Some time later the holy man comes back down the path and finds his disciple, bruised and thin. What happened to you? You told me not to bite, the snake says. So I didn't. And look at me. And the holy man answers: I told you not to bite. I never told you not to hiss. That's the line. Ramakrishna draws it out for the people in the room. Someone living in the world, he says, should harm no one. But they may need to raise a hiss, to show a little spirit, so that others don't take advantage. The hiss isn't the bite. It's a boundary you show, not a wound you give. Notice how this sits next to the man we met yesterday, the one who wept for God. Ramakrishna is a mystic, but in M.'s pages he is also strikingly practical. He knows his visitors are going home to offices, households and people who push. He doesn't tell them to stop being gentle. He tells them that gentle and defenseless are not the same thing. That's what reading the Gospel in selections is like: talk of the Divine Mother one moment, and the next, advice from a snake.
screen: `STOP BITING. HARM NO ONE.` · `THE BOYS WHIRL IT BY THE TAIL.` · `I NEVER TOLD YOU NOT TO HISS.` · then, large: `A HISS IS NOT A BITE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Bring to mind one place where you've been letting yourself get walked on: at work, at home, online. Don't rehearse a fight. Just breathe, and imagine calmly what a hiss would sound like there: one clear sentence, one boundary, said without wanting to hurt anyone. Hold that sentence gently, the way you'd hold something you might need later. Then let it go, and rest in the breath. If you pray, you can ask for the courage to say it kindly. The bell holds the time.
Ramakrishna. The mystic of Dakshineswar who could talk of God in one breath and, in the next, tell a snake it was allowed to hiss.
Your line: I never told you not to hiss. Today, if someone pushes too far, hiss without biting: one calm, clear boundary, and no harm done. Day nine hundred thirty-six.

937.title: Ramakrishna (the Gospel, selections)
937.hook: a doll made of salt walks into the sea to measure how deep it is
937.howItsDone: Devotees read the Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna in study circles and at centers of the Ramakrishna order, and his parables, like the salt doll, are retold in talks and at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramakrishna's snake that stopped biting and was told, I never told you not to hiss. Did you need a hiss, without the bite? Day nine hundred thirty-seven.

A doll made entirely of salt sets out to measure the ocean. It's a small doll with a big job: find out how deep the water goes, then come back and report. It walks down to the shore. It steps in. And right there the story stops being about measuring, because the moment the doll is in the water, it starts to dissolve. Ramakrishna told this little parable when people asked him a question that sounds simple: what is God like, really? Today, why a teacher who talked about God all day long answered with a doll that never comes back.
screen: `A DOLL MADE OF SALT.` → `IT GOES TO MEASURE THE OCEAN.` → `IT NEVER COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: The visitors who came to Ramakrishna's room were often educated men, used to debating. They wanted a definition. He gave them pictures instead, and the Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna, the book of his conversations, is full of them. The salt doll is one. It went to measure the ocean, and it melted. So who was left to come back and say how deep it was? That is his answer about Brahman, the reality the Upanishads point to beyond every name. You can't stand outside it and take its measurements, because the one measuring is made of the same stuff. Get close enough, and the measurer is gone. In the Gospel he makes the same point another way, and it's startling. Everything, he says, has become uchchhishta, a word for food that has already been tasted: leftovers. The Vedas, the scriptures, the philosophies have all passed through human mouths, so in that sense they've been tasted. Only one thing has never been made leftover, and that is Brahman, because no one has ever been able to say what it is. Notice what he isn't saying. He isn't throwing scripture away. He sang hymns, he quoted the sacred books, and he worshiped the Mother in the temple. He's saying that words point, and what they point to is bigger than any mouth. And the parable isn't a sad one. The doll goes into the ocean because it wants to know. Some readers add that a doll of salt came from the sea in the first place. Its not coming back is the answer.
screen: `THE SALT DOLL MELTS.` · `NO ONE COMES BACK TO REPORT.` · `EVERYTHING ELSE IS LEFTOVERS.` · `WORDS POINT; THEY DON'T CONTAIN.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind something you love that you've never managed to explain well: a person, a place, a piece of music, or, if you pray, God. Try, silently, to describe it in one sentence. Notice how the sentence falls short. Then let the sentence go, and simply stay near the thing itself, the way the doll stood at the water's edge. There's nothing to measure. Just stay close. The bell holds the time.
Ramakrishna. The temple priest at Dakshineswar who answered hard questions with small pictures. Today's picture: the salt doll that went to measure the ocean.
Your line: the measurer is gone. Today, when something good won't fit into words, let it stay unworded, and enjoy it anyway. Day nine hundred thirty-seven.

938.title: Ramakrishna (the Gospel, selections)
938.hook: three friends argue about the color of a lizard on a tree, and the man who lives under it settles it
938.carry: every color, and sometimes no color at all
938.howItsDone: Ramakrishna's parables, like the chameleon on the tree, are retold in talks at Ramakrishna order centers, in study circles that read the Gospel together, and at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramakrishna and the salt doll that went to measure the ocean and never came back to report, and the measurer is gone. Did anything stay happily unworded? Day nine hundred thirty-eight.

Red. I saw it myself, it was red. No, it was green, I was standing right there. You're both wrong, it was blue. Three friends, one tree, one small lizard, and an argument getting louder by the minute. Each of them went into the woods, saw a chameleon on a branch, and came back certain. Ramakrishna told this story to the visitors in his room at Dakshineswar, and the one who settles it isn't any of the three. Today, the man who lives under the tree.

In the Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna, the quarrel goes on until they all walk back to the tree to settle it. A man is sitting underneath. Yes, he says, I live here, and I know that creature well. Every one of you is right. Sometimes it's red, sometimes green, sometimes yellow or blue. And sometimes it has no color at all. Ramakrishna gives the meaning plainly. The one who thinks of God constantly, he says, comes to know God's real nature, and knows that God shows himself to seekers in many forms and aspects: with qualities, and then again without any. Only the man under the tree knows the lizard can be every color, and sometimes none. It's the others, he says, who suffer through useless arguments. Notice what the man under the tree does not say. He doesn't tell anyone they made it up. Each friend really did see red, or green. The trouble came with one extra word: only. And notice where his knowledge comes from. Not from a sharper argument, but from living there. Yesterday's salt doll walked into the ocean and never came back to describe it. The man under the tree has the same kind of authority: closeness, not cleverness. And the last thing he says, sometimes no color at all, points to where the salt doll went. That closes a week. It began with Mira's ledger, a treasure that grows when it's spent, went out into the lanes of Bengal with Chaitanya's drums, and came to rest in a room at Dakshineswar, where a priest answered questions with a pond, a snake, a doll made of salt, and a lizard on a tree. Tomorrow, one of the young men who sat in that room stands up to speak a very long way from home.
screen: `THE MAN UNDER THE TREE.` · `EVERY ONE OF YOU IS RIGHT.` · `SOMETIMES NO COLOR AT ALL.` · `CLOSENESS, NOT CLEVERNESS.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind someone you've disagreed with about something that matters to you both: God, a family story, the right way to live. Let their version be red and yours be green. Don't decide who's right. Just ask, quietly: what did they actually see, from where they were standing? Stay with that question for a few breaths. Then rest a moment in what neither of you has seen yet, the part with no color at all. If you pray, you can hold that person in a prayer you already know. The bell holds the time.
Ramakrishna. The priest of Dakshineswar, telling of a lizard on a tree that shows every color, and sometimes no color at all.
Your line: every color, and sometimes no color at all. Today, when someone describes a thing differently from you, ask what they saw before you tell them what you saw. Day nine hundred thirty-eight.
